title: Time & Work; Pipes & Cisterns
relevance: Campus aptitude OAs and technical screens routinely test time-work and pipes-cisterns, often rewrapped as servers, threads, or agents processing work.

phases.goal: Establish the LCM/Total Work method and the MDH equation as the default integer-rate framing.

must_hit.point: Define Total Work as the LCM of the given times so each worker's rate is an integer (Total Work / time).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says take LCM of the times as total units, then rate = total/time, not starting from 1/A fractions.

must_hit.point: Combined rate is the sum of individual rates; time to finish is Total Work divided by combined rate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States add rates, then time = Total Work / combined rate.

must_hit.point: For men, days, and hours with fixed work, use the MDH relation M1×D1×H1/W1 = M2×D2×H2/W2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes or cites the MDH equation equating man-day-hour effort per unit work across scenarios.

probes: Instead of working with 1/A and 1/B, how do you set up a time-and-work problem using total work and rates?
When the inputs are numbers of people, days, and hours per day, what equation do you use?

hints.1: Think about choosing a convenient unit for the whole job rather than fractions per day.
hints.2: Total Work is the LCM of the given times; rate is that total divided by each person's time.
hints.3: Total Work = LCM(t1,t2,…); rate = Total Work/time; combined rate = sum of rates; time = Total Work/combined rate; groups use M1 D1 H1 / W1 = M2 D2 H2 / W2.

phases.goal: Apply LCM rates to combined workers, leftover work, pairwise sums, efficiency ratios, MDH scaling, wages, alternate days, and early leavers.

must_hit.point: With A in 10 days and B in 15 days, LCM total 30 gives rates 3 and 2, combined 5, so together they finish in 6 days.
From pairwise rates (A+B), (B+C), (C+A), summing yields twice (A+B+C), so divide by 2 to get the triple combined rate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Adds the three pair rates and halves to get A+B+C, then divides total work by that rate.

must_hit.point: Efficiency and time are inverse: if A is 30% more efficient than B, A:B efficiency is 13:10 so time ratio is 10:13.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Converts 30% more into 130:100 = 13:10, then flips for time and solves with B's given days.

must_hit.point: Wages for people working the same duration split in their efficiency (rate) ratio, not equally.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Takes LCM-based rates, forms rate shares of total pay (e.g. B gets 3/9 of the purse).

must_hit.point: On alternate days, work in full A-then-B cycles, then finish the remainder day-by-day (possibly a fractional last day).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses cycle work, floor of full cycles, then assigns remaining units to the next workers in order.

must_hit.point: If someone leaves x days before completion, add the work they would have done in those x days to Total Work, then divide by the all-workers combined rate ("didn't leave" trick).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Inflates total work by the missed contributions and divides by the full combined rate to get total days.

probes: A finishes in 10 days, B in 15; how long together, using LCM total work?
A+B, B+C, and C+A times are given—how do you find how long all three take together?
Someone leaves a few days before the job ends; how can you still solve with one combined-rate division?

hints.1: Stay in integer units from the LCM; avoid mixing fractions mid-problem.
hints.2: Pairs: sum of pair rates = 2×(A+B+C). Early leave: pretend they stayed and add their missed work to the total.
hints.3: Example shape: LCM, rates, sum or half of pair sums; for leave-x-early, adjusted total = original + x×rate_left, time = adjusted/combined.

phases.goal: Contrast LCM integer rates vs unit-fraction rates, and inlet (positive) vs outlet/leak (negative) rate signs.

must_hit.point: Prefer defining Total Work as LCM of times over computing fractional work per day like 1/A, because rates stay clean integers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly chooses LCM total units instead of starting from 1/A, 1/B fractions.

must_hit.point: Filling pipes get positive rates; emptying pipes or leaks get negative rates—blindly adding all rates as positive answers a different problem.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Assigns + to inlets and − to outlets/leaks before combining, and mentions the MCQ trap of treating the outlet as positive.

probes: Why use an LCM total-work setup instead of working only with 1/A-type fractions?
In a tank with fill pipes and an emptying pipe or leak, how do you treat the rates when combining?

hints.1: One approach keeps arithmetic integer; the other keeps unit fractions.
hints.2: LCM turns every rate into Total/time; outlets must reduce the net fill rate.
hints.3: Total Work = LCM(...); fill rates positive, empty/leak negative; net rate = sum with signs; time = capacity/net.

phases.goal: Map the same LCM-rate model onto pipes/cisterns and OA wrappers (servers, swarms) including crashes and jammers-as-outlets.

must_hit.point: Pipes and cisterns use the same LCM capacity and rates; an emptying pipe or leak is a negative rate (e.g. fill + empty together: +5,+4,−3 → net 6).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sets tank capacity to LCM, signs outlet negative, divides capacity by net rate.

must_hit.point: If a fill pipe alone takes 10 hours but with a leak takes 15 hours, leak rate is effective rate minus fill rate (negative), and empty-alone time is capacity over that magnitude.
must_hit.evidence_hint: LCM(10,15)=30; A=+3; effective=+2; leak=−1; empty time 30 hours.

must_hit.point: OA wrappers (servers processing a batch, drone swarms vs a jammer) are identical math: workers as inlets, corruption/crash as partial leave or an outlet.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Restates server/swarm wording as standard combined work or two-inlets-one-outlet, then applies LCM rates.

probes: Two fill pipes and one emptying pipe open together—how long to fill, and what is the trap in the options?
Server Alpha and Beta process a batch together until Beta crashes mid-job; how do you find total time?
Two mapping swarms plus a jammer that ruins a full map over a fixed time—what rates do you assign?

hints.1: Rename the story back to workers and pipes; the equations do not change.
hints.2: Crash after t minutes = together for t, then one rate on the remainder; jammer = negative rate.
hints.3: LCM capacity; positive process/map rates; jammer negative; for crash: together work then remainder/survivor rate; add the two time segments.

tradeoffs.topic: LCM total-work rates vs fractional 1/A per day
tradeoffs.strong_answer: LCM of the given times as Total Work makes each rate Total/time an integer, combined rate a simple sum, and finish time Total/combined—cleaner than carrying unit fractions throughout.

Fill pipes and productive workers contribute positive units per time; emptying pipes, leaks, or jammers contribute negative rates. Net rate is the signed sum; treating an outlet as positive computes the wrong scenario.
Time is inversely proportional to efficiency. A percentage efficiency advantage (e.g. 30% more → 13:10) flips when converting to days, then scale with the given person's time.

gotchas.trap: Adding an emptying pipe or leak as a positive rate along with the fill pipes.
gotchas.correction: Assign a negative rate to outlets/leaks; net fill rate is sum with signs. Blind positive addition is a classic wrong MCQ path.

gotchas.trap: Trying to piece-wise model early leavers without a clear timeline and getting stuck.
gotchas.correction: Use the didn't-leave trick: add the work the early leavers would have done in the days they missed to Total Work, then divide by the full combined rate.

gotchas.trap: On alternate-day work, stopping after whole cycles or forgetting who works the leftover units.
gotchas.correction: Finish full A-then-B cycles, subtract completed units, then continue day by day (or fraction of a day) in the stated starting order until the remainder is done.

gotchas.trap: Splitting wages equally when people worked the same calendar time but have different rates.
gotchas.correction: With equal duration together, pay shares follow the efficiency (rate) ratio from the LCM setup.
